newsitem.title: INDIA: Boart, Unicorp see 25 pct share in India.
newsitem.headline: Boart, Unicorp see 25 pct share in India.

text.p: A new firm set up by South Africa's Boart Longyear Group and India's Unicorp Industries, said on Wednesday it expected to get 25 percent of India's mining equipment market in the products it would sell.

Boart Longyear, a unit of the Anglo American Industrial Corp, will hold 51 percent and Unicorp 49 percent in the firm, Boart Longyear Unicorp Ltd, officials from the two partners told a news conference announcing the firm's launch in New Delhi.

The firm, which would invest 40 million rupees ($1.12 milion), is yet to get approval from India's Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB), but hopes to start work this year as no hitches are expected in getting the approval, they said.
Rakesh Dewan, the new company's managing director-designate, said the firm expected sales of 500 million rupees ($14 million) in the domestic market in three years' time.
"Initially, manufacturing will be export-oriented," said Hilton Davies, Boart Longyear's group chairman.
The company would first make pneumatic hand-held rock drills, Davies said. "We will add to the manufacturing base once the demand expands," he added.
"A wide range of products will be offered by the new company including capital equipment, rock drilling tools and certain diamond products," Unicorp said in a statement.

Davies said India would become the 31st country to serve as a manufacturing base for Boart Longyear, and added that the equipment it made in India would be a part of the group's global manufacturing activity.

The Indian plant was expected to have an advantage in cost-effective labour services, particularly in engineering, Davies said. "You have a very low cost-labour ratio. You have excellent engineers here," he said.
Davies said Boart Longyear saw an emerging opporutunity in coal mining in India after New Delh announced on Tuesday a new policy to allow private investment in coal exploration.
"We are number one in exploration drilling. That is one area we will be looking at (in India)," Davies said.

Dewan said the company would initially make diamond-based tools for surface use in various mining industries including granite, marble, iron ore, copper and zinc but expected to later manufacture equipment for drilling in depths.

He identified Atlas Copco, Sandvik Asia, Widia India and Ingersoll Rand among the key competitors for Boart Longyear Unicorp in the Indian market, but added that the same competitors were present worldwide, too.
Unicorp Industries, which also has interests in computer manufacture, had a turnover of 1.5 billion rupees ($41.9 million) in the year that ended in September 1996.
"It is expected to achieve a turnover of 10 billion rupees by the year 2000," its statement said.
Boart Longyear reported a turnover of $800 million in 1995, the statement said.
In July 1995, the two companies had forged a marketing alliance to sell Boart equipment used in mining of metals, coal, granite and marble as well as in infrastructure sectors like power and roads.
Davies said the manufacturing venture followed as a consequence. "We felt that we should taste the waters," he said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
